utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. Good morning, everybody. All the accused are here. Prosecution today is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Elderkin. Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Lazarevic, Mr. Josse, Ms. Nikolic, and Mr. Haynes. All right. Any preliminaries? Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I hadn't planned on standing up before you, but since we have the occasion without a witness in the room, I would like to take care of one housekeeping matter. That pertains to the Trial Chamber's oral decision of 10 October 2008 concerning the admission of a 92 bis statement by Petar Loncarevic, and we have completed the formalities in relation to that statement. It has been uploaded on to e-court as 4D644. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell, for that information. Anything else? I saw Mr. McCloskey about to stand. Yes, he is standing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We had the last witness where I think we hadn't done the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we're ready to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. That's not what I meant with preliminaries. No, no. We still have got to deal with the documents. Okay. No other preliminaries? So, documents. We had admitted, I think, one document or two documents, no? Or three?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Chairman, I sent the list of about 60 documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Then any objection? Go slowly if you're going to object to several, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. There is one document that did not have an ERN on it, but we don't have an objection to that. We are looking a little bit more into it, but at this time we don't have any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Other Defence teams, any objections? We hear none. So all these documents are admitted. Which one is it? Is it the last one, 5D1411?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That last one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- is part of a report, and we are tracking that down and we don't have a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Registrar, also, there are three at least that I can see of those documents that have not yet been translated; and, consequently, they will be marked for identification pending translation thereof. Okay? There are no other Defence teams wishing to tender any documents? Yes. Then we'll move to the Prosecution list. It has been circulated, too. Any objections, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci. Other Defence teams, any objection? None. So all these documents are also admitted. I am not aware of pending translations, as at least as it appears from that list. But while you were cross-examining this witness, I think there were several documents that had not yet been translated. These have all not yet been translated. So all those documents that have not yet been translated will remain marked for identification purposes until they are duly translated. Thank you. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would just like to say for the record, Mr. President, that our consent to the admission of these documents, of course, is subject to the caveat of our motion, which is currently pending before the Trial Chamber, concerning the documents adduced by the Prosecution. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Thank you. It goes without saying, I mean, by now, after two and a half years, you should have a familiarised yourself with our system. Okay. So let's bring the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal. Before you start giving evidence as a Defence witness, our rules require from you a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. That is the solemn declaration that you have in front of you, please read it out aloud, and that will be your undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. You are going to be asked some questions by Mr. Petrusic for General Miletic, and then we will see who else would like to put questions to you. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. As you've just heard, my name is Nenad Petrusic, and I represent the Defence of General Miletic and will be asking you some questions today. But before that, I would like to ask you to state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: My name is Nedeljko Ilic. I was born in 1950, in Tegare, in the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ilic, could you please tell us what schools have you completed?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: I am an economist; I completed the vocational college of economics.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And do you work today?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: I work in my son's company; it's a privately run business.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Before the armed conflict broke out in the territory of the Republic of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina, did you work?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did work in the Podrinje Company; it's a catering tourist business. It was also before these events occurred and afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ilic, I would like to ask you to make a pause before starting your answer so that everything is interpreted.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where were the headquarters of your company located?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: The hotel catering tourist company Podrinje had its headquarters in Bratunac. In addition to hotels, the company included restaurants and other facilities, so it was a company that dealt with catering and tourism.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that at page 4, line 25, we have an obvious mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It will be looked into and corrected. Thank you for pointing it out. Thank you. It's basically for the record, instead of the witness's name "Nedeljko Ilic," we have "Slavko Novakovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ilic, did your company continue operating throughout the war between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes. We worked throughout that at a period. We served the third persons to a smaller degree, but we mostly catered to the needs of the military and civilian authorities as they asked us to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And when the war broke out, were you mobilized, conscripted into the army Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, from April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And were you in the army throughout that time?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the beginning until the end; until 1995, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And did you at the same time perform your job at the company?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I was conscripted in such a way that I had to do some work for my company; and then, as needed, I was used or deployed in the Bratunac Brigade as they needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When we are talking about the outbreak of the hostilities in 1992, the line between your unit -- actually, who were you fighting?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: The separation line was the Zuti Most, Yellow Bridge, Zagan [as interpreted], and so on, between Srebrenica and Bratunac; and the conflict broke out between Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And those two municipalities, Bratunac and Srebrenica, were they adjacent?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ilic, do you know that at some point in time during the war protected areas were set up in that region?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that from mid-1993 onwards, that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us what was the protected area?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: That was the area that covered the Srebrenica municipality, and it was adjacent to the area covered by the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And do you know what peacekeeping force came to the municipality of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: I know that, first, there were some smaller units; I don't know much about them. And in the second half of 1993, towards the end of 1993, the Dutch Battalion was deployed there as the peacekeeping force in the Srebrenica protected area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you have any business or private relations with the peacekeeping force?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Upon the arrival of the Dutch Battalion in late 1993, I was told that there was a possibility that I might be providing them with logistics support from my company. There was a number of meetings in the regiments, and this was, indeed, agreed upon later. So those were the contacts that I had with the Dutch Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us how did those meetings come about? What were the needs of the two sides?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Well, the representative of the observers - I think his name was Andres - he came to the Fontana Hotel with Mr. Nikolic, and they said that they had problems with supplying the forces up there at Potocari, deployed there at Potocari, in terms of logistics. They asked me whether I could organise at the level of the company the logistics support for them. And since there were problems and difficulties, I also had to contact the civilian authorities, tell them about it. I also had to contact the military authorities, and they gave me the permission to set up a meeting and to agree about this business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Not an objection, but I see a reference to Mr. Nikolic and thought it might be helpful that that's cleared up before we go any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are talking about of Momir Nikolic, though, aren't we? I just need a confirmation and we can proceed. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ilic, could you please tell us which Nikolic are you talking about, the one that attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: That was Mr. Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what did this logistics support imply, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Well, the logistics support comprised the provision of food stuffs, bread, fruit, vegetables, juice, beer, cans, and other food stuffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 5D1170 up on the screen, and could we move to page 2 of this document in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ilic, in this version, in the Serbian version, do you recognise the signature on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: It is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now go back to page 1 in both versions of this contract.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us if you recall this contract on the provision of catering services?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The date on this contract is the 18th of March, 1994. So was that the first contract that you concluded with the representatives of UNPROFOR, and of the Dutch Battalion, to be more specific?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was the first contract, the first final contract that was signed. The other meetings were of a preparatory nature, and technicalities were arranged, the kind and prices for the goods to be supplied and other technical issues that had to be dealt with before the goods were actually delivered. So all the details were arranged that there would be twice weekly deliveries, the items to be supplied were specified, and it was also specified that payment would be cash on delivery.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like us to look at 5D1171. Could we please have it up on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ilic, as you sit here, given the time that has passed in the meantime, do you recall this document?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is an approval given by the government for cooperation and work with the Dutch Battalion. It was signed by the finance minister, Milenko Stanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We can see in this information bulletin that some goods could not be procured. Could you please tell us what this meant?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, this had to do with the procurement of weapons, footwear, clothes, and military equipment. I think that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In accordance with the contract that you signed with the members of the Dutch Battalion, and pursuant to this memo of the government, you did not have any restrictions on the provision of supplies?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Up until I received this document, I could not do anything. It was only when I received this document from the government that I was able to actually provide the services as per the contract to the members of the Dutch Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have document 5D525. In the English version, the date is wrong; and instead of the 18th of March, 1994, it actually should read the 18th of March, 1995. Could we please go to page 2 of this document, in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ilic, tell us, do you recognise the signature on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We can go back to page 1, where the representative of the Dutch Battalion is said to be Major Boering. Do you remember this officer who was the representative of DutchBat when this contract was concluded?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes, I remember this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ilic, you had a previous contract which was valid in 1984 and the date was 18th of March, but it was 1994. Now we have another one dated the 18th of March, 1995. Can you explain why the same contract was concluded again? It's same as regards the rights and obligations of both parties to the contract.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: As the first contract had expired, it was valid for only a year. After a year of work, the parties had to decide whether they would continue their operation or not. As both parties were satisfied, a new contract was drawn up on the 18th of March, 1995, after the expiry of the one-year contract.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In line 6, page 11, its 1984, not 1984.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you remember for what period this contract was concluded?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: You mean this last one, the 18th of March, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it was valid for a year, also.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Under this contract also, did you deliver to DutchBat goods once or twice a week under the same conditions as previously?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, and they were satisfied. We even discussed extending our cooperation so that they could reside in the Fontana Hotel in a more organised manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 5D1172 on the screen, please. Could we scroll down a little bit in the Serbian version. Excellent, yes. Very good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ilic, do you recognise this signature on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is about and whether it has any connection with your business dealings with UNPROFOR or, rather, with DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: This document is a report on the business done with the DutchBat over a particular period of time. We were obliged to send such a report to the government and to the military authorities, so both to the civilian and the military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have document 1173 -- 5D - excuse me - 1173.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ilic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is an invoice where the goods delivered are listed, beer, coca cola, juice, and cake; the delivery dates; it says that the goods were paid for in cash; and the representative of UNPROFOR who took delivery of the goods and paid for them is mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was this carried out on the 5th of May, 1995, this takeover of goods and the payment?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, certainly. The 5th of May. Because on the day the goods were delivered, the invoice was drawn up and the payment made; and then for the next order, we would go across the Yellow Bridge to the UNPROFOR headquarters, to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to whether the representatives of DutchBat, when they took delivery of the goods, until the time they crossed the Yellow Bridge, had any limitations -- or, rather, were the goods checked, were they confiscated, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of that. Probably, the representative of DutchBat would have told us if he had had any problems. When they took delivery of the goods, there was always a commission that included a representative of the brigade and a representative of the municipality, so that when the invoice was finished, the representative of the brigade would escort them as far as the demarcation line or the separation line. I think there were no problems in this respect because, certainly, had there been any problems, they would have pointed that out when they came to the Fontana Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like another document, 5D1293.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ilic, do you remember this document?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of July 1995 is when this document was issued, and the title of the document is "Authorisation to Fontana Hotel Bratunac to Provide Commercial Services to UNPROFOR." So it's an authorisation. Did you continue providing UNPROFOR with your services?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. And from the document, you can see that the representatives of the Drina Corps agreed for this business deal to be continued. So, on the 1st of July, 1995, as this document shows, the business deal continued to function.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In addition to these deals that you had based on those two contracts, did representatives of DutchBat visit your hotel and make use of other hotel services?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: I think they did and I don't think there were any obstacles to that. I was even invited to visit their command. They visited the hotel without any problems. They had no problems either in the hotel itself or in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In mid-July, were you in the hotel? Were you at work?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: No. As of the 4th of July, I was in my unit of the Bratunac Brigade, that was the R Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions in my examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I have no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No questions, Mr. President. Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good morning, witness. My name is Rupert Elderkin, and I am going to ask you a few questions on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can we have, please, 65 ter number 4070.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So you see this letter dated 18th of March, 1994. This is a letter that you wrote; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote this, or, rather, my secretary; and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And this is the same date as the first contract that you signed with DutchBat, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes. The 18th of March 1994, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And in this letter, you sought permission from the local military authorities in Bratunac to sell, it says, "beer, wine, and provisions," to the DutchBat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And you also wrote: "With such dealings, we would achieve economic effects that would be beneficial for both parties." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That's correct. Part of the profits went to the brigade and part went to the company. It was wartime and the company did only a little business with third persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 4075, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: While that's coming up, could you say how much of the profit was going to the Bratunac Brigade, a percentage?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Okay. You can see now there is another document on the screen which is dated the 28th of June, 1995. This is a message that you wrote to the Drina Corps command --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are receiving translation in French on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Apologies by interpreters. Apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Please go ahead and sorry for the interruption, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So this is a document from the 28th of June, 1995, which you wrote to the Drina Corps command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And with this document, you are requesting permission from General Zivanovic to continue to trade with DutchBat; that's right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And you see there is a remark, and this says: "You do know that this business cooperation allows for the logical support of the Bratunac Brigade with 70 per cent profits, and that it has been planned that the 300.000.000 dinars are given to that brigade by the end of the year." So the Bratunac Brigade received most of the profits from the trade with DutchBat, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes, 70 per cent went to them and the plan was earn 300.000 dinars.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 4071, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Okay. This is going back now to 1994, and this is a document from the 5th of August. This is a request that you sent - you with the president of the Bratunac municipal Assembly sent - asking whether the VRS Main Staff had consented for the Podrinje company to trade with DutchBat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am familiar with the document, and this is how it was. We were duty-bound to send this to the General Staff and to the government, all this information, and ask them to approve our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So I see in the English, it refers to General Staff. That is the Main Staff of the VRS, as in the staff headed by General Mladic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 4072, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now this is a document from the 10th of August of 1994, and this is a document sent by the Drina Corps command to the Bratunac Brigade command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And the Drina Corps command is responding to the 5th of August letter we have just seen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And here the Drina Corps command says: "The command of the VRS Main Staff (Logistics Sector) has given their consent for the goods to be delivered under the following conditions ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And you agree that the trading relationship between the Podrinje company and DutchBat was subject to this consent of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, both the Main Staff and the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could we see again 65 ter 5D1171, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now, we have already looked at this document this morning. This is an information bulletin dated 30th of March, 1994, from the Republika Srpska Ministry of Trade and Supply. Now, you saw this document earlier, and page 10, lines 15 to 18 said: "Up until I received this document, I could not do anything. It was only when I received this document from the government that I was able to actually provide the services as per the contract." Correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Without both of these approvals, I wouldn't be able to work. There may be a mistake in the dates somewhere, but that's how it was. Without this information or advice from the government, without their approval, that is, and from the brigade, I couldn't do that. I couldn't engage in that business deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now, this document also refers to goods which your company was not permitted to trade with DutchBat; and in response to a question about that, you said, at page 10, lines 9 to 11, that: "Well, for the most part, this had to do with the procurement of weapons, footwear, clothes, and military equipment. I think that's what it was." Do you recall that answer?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now, in fact, this document here before us refers to a list of goods at Article 2 of the decree on special conditions of traffic of goods and services in the Official Gazette of the Republika Srpska, number 1693. You see that reference?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if we could have, please, 65 ter 4079.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While that is coming up, Mr. Elderkin, the break will be at 10.40 and not at 10.30. That will be a shortened break of the 20 minutes instead of the usual 25. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And I may be done by then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down on the B/C/S page. And I see in the English, there doesn't appear to be a second page. There should be a translation of Article 2. It should be page 2. Perfect. Article 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And so you see this is the decree which was referred to in the letter from the ministry we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: I think this refers to the needs of the military: Maize, wheat, beans, salt, detergents, and so on, lard. There was no need for me to deal in that, nor did I. One can see that from the specifications on the invoices that were issued when the representatives of DutchBat took delivery of the goods. The goods listed here in Article 2 are not mentioned in any of the invoices.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, sir. I just wanted to take this logically so that it's as clear to us as it is to you. But this is the decree on special conditions of traffic and goods and services which was referred to in the letter we just saw; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And do you recall that the letter specified that the Podrinje company was not permitted to trade the goods listed in Article 2 of this decree with DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: They didn't list them by kind. It was only mentioned that Article 2 from the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska listed goods. My people in my office had that Official Gazette and we abided by it. So we traded only in goods we were permitted to trade in by the staff, Main Staff, and by the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And you already, in fact, referred to the goods listed in Article 2, and those included wheat, wheat flour, corn, corn flour, sugar, oil, lard, beans, salt, rice, and dairy products, as well as other basic goods, and anything else which the ministry might decide; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is true because these were strategic commodities, and the ministry decided there. There was no need for us to ask for that, to request it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And you were not permitted to sell these strategic commodities to the DutchBat according to the letter from the ministry that we just saw; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could we see 65 ter 4073, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now, this is a bill from the Podrinje company to UNPROFOR, dated the 17th of February 1995, and signed by yourself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And on this occasion, the goods sold to DutchBat were beer, wine, and soft drinks; that's right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And no food appears on this bill?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: No, there is no food there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could we see again 5D1173, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And we already looked at this bill which is from the 5th of May; and, here, the goods that were sold to DutchBat were beer, juice, soft drinks, and some cake. No other food appears on the bill apart from the cake, does it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: That's correct, just cakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If we could have 5D1172, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now, again, we've already seen this document this morning. Could you tell us what period does this report cover, please?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: I think that the reports were submitted quarterly, every three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And this report shows the profits that were being made by the Podrinje company under the contract with DutchBat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: But it does not identify which goods were actually -- which kind of goods were actually being sold, does it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Since copies of bills were sent both to the brigade and the municipal authorities, the itemized reports they had; but this is a summary report based on those invoices and bills. So this is a quarterly report for the business that was done in the three month periods, item by item.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 4074, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now, this is an information report dated the 2nd of May 1995. Who was this sent to?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: We were under an obligation to send those documents to the military and civilian authorities, to the government, and to the General Staff, too. And this is for the period from the 1st of March 1995 until the 1st of May 1995, so it's a two-month period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, in fact, this shows all of the sales made by the Podrinje company to DutchBat during that two-month period; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And the total value of those sales was over 102.000 Deutschmarks, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And more than half of that was from sales of beer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, in fact, almost all of the sales were of drinks, more than 100.000 Deutschmarks; and apart from drinks, the only sales of food was of cakes, which was for the value of some 1.500 Deutschmarks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now, at page 8, lines 24 to 25, today, you said: "The logistics support comprised the provision of food stuffs, bread, fruit, vegetables, beer, cans, and other food stuffs." Now, the only food stuffs we've seen sold to DutchBat in these invoices is cake, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Well, you probably don't have the invoices, but food and vegetables, all the food stuffs that were not listed in Article 2 of the Official Gazette, the ones that couldn't be traded, they were sold. You probably just don't have the relevant invoices, but I do think that deliveries were made of fruit, vegetables, and cakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Elderkin. Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ilic, in the course of your business cooperation with the Dutch Battalion, did there come a time that they -- when they asked you to deliver goods, that you were not able to deliver to them?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ILIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think so. They also were aware of our capabilities and of all those things, so that they did not make any special request that we would not be able to meet, apart from the goods that are listed in Article 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Ilic, we have no further questions for you. We are finished with your testimony. You are free to go. Our staff will assist you and facilitate your return back home at the earliest. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over and also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll do the documents after the break; make sure you have them ready. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, documents. Mr. Petrusic, you have five documents which I see here on the list. Any objection from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: None, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And from the other Defence teams? So thank you. These documents are all admitted. Then we have the Prosecution list, seven documents. Any objections, Ms. Fauveau -- sorry, Mr. Petrusic? Pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. Any objections from the other Defence teams? None. So these seven documents are also admitted, and we can move to the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you're most welcome at this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence as a Defence witness for General Miletic. Before you do so, our rules require that you make a solemn declaration to the effect that you will be testifying the truth. A text is being given to you now, please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. You will be asked some questions by -- please make yourself comfortable. You will be asked some questions by Ms. Fauveau, and then we will see who else will have some questions for you. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you let's know your name?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: My name is Maja Spiroski, nee Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What was your education, which studies did you do?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: I have a degree in dentistry, and I specialised in dental prosthetics.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What is your connection with General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: He is my father.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What is your birth date?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: I was born on the 10th of July, 1977, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was born in Zadar, the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Well, I declare myself as a Serb, but I have both Croatian and the Serbian citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What is the nationality of your mother?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, my mother is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you have a brother or a sister?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I have a brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I am married.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What is the nationality of your husband?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: My husband is Macedonian, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is your brother married?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Yes, he is married.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What is the nationality of the wife of your brother, or brother's wife?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: His wife is a Croat, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Where did you live before the beginning of war in ex-Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Up until the beginning of the war, we lived in Zadar, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell us in which year you left Zadar?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: We left Zadar in the summer of 1991, right at the beginning of the summer of that year.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: With whom did you live in Zadar during the last year before you left Zadar?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Well, the last year, 1991, before we had left, and in the last part of 1990, my mother, my brother, and myself lived in Zadar. My father was away in Belgrade for his studies, so he was not with us that year.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell us why you left Zadar? Why did you leave Zadar?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Well, in 1991, it was a very difficult year. It was a period of unrest throughout Croatia, but it was felt for the most part in Zadar, because the population there was of mixed ethnicity, and there was a lot of army personnel there. So I remember this whole year as a series of unpleasant situations at school, and in our environment in general. But at that time, I was not so much offended by what people were saying about Serbs, because I did not feel at that time that I was a Serb. I felt that I was a Yugoslav, and it didn't matter to me what ethnic background people had. Whereas, what people were saying about the Yugoslav Peoples' Army and the military personnel in general, that really I found it, because I took it personally as attacks on my father and by extension on our whole family.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you left Zadar in 1991, who were you with? With whom did you leave?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: I left Zadar with my brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What happened about your mother, for your mother?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: My mom remained in Zadar for a while, up until September or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Why did your mother stay in Zadar after you left?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Well, my mom had a job in Zadar; on the other hand, we were a typical [as interpreted] army family. We did not follow our father as he was moving from post to post. My mom worked in Zadar and my brother and I went to school, and we expected that things would calm down and that we would go back to Zadar. My brother was about to start his university studies, so the situation for him was a little bit different, but I expected fully that I would go back to Zadar to reunite with my mother because nobody really expected the war to break out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please go asked slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau, will you look into that, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would ask you to speak a bit slower, because the interpreters have some problems. You are speaking a bit too fast, much too fast. And also, for the transcript, I think there is a mistake at page 28, lines 6 and 7. Could you repeat what you said. You were a family -- a typical family of militaries, or non-typical family of militaries?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: We were not a typical army family. In the course of their service, army personnel would be moved from post to post and their families usually followed them; but up until the age of 13, from my birth, and my brother up until his 20th year, we lived in Zadar and so did my mother. My father was with us unless he was posted somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that your brother was supposed to start his studies. Where did he go to when he left Zadar?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: My brother went to Sarajevo, to the university there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Why did he choose to go to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Well, both brothers and sister of my father lived in Sarajevo, so that my brother and I would always spend at least a part of your summer and winter vacations in Sarajevo. So it was quite natural that once we started our university studies that we would do that in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What happened, where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Well, at the time when we left Sarajevo, my brother and I, we were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: When we left Zadar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- my brother and I, we went to Sarajevo. My brother remained in town for a while, and I went to stay with my father's relatives in the country -- in the countryside. Then we went back to Sarajevo. It became clear that at that time we would not be going back to Zadar, and we were trying to find some solution for my education. At the time, I was about to enroll in secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And, finally, where did you go to secondary school?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: In the end, I went to the secondary school in Belgrade. It was a dentistry school.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What were your first impressions in Belgrade? How did you get used to living in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Well, I found it hard to accommodate to life in Belgrade. Belgrade is much bigger than the town where I grew up, and I had problems at school at the time. Well, language was the same, but the script was the problem for me. Because in Serbia, Cyrillic was used much more. I didn't really know it, because in Croatia we mostly used the Latin alphabet. So, right at the beginning, I had some problems while I was coming to terms with the Cyrillic alphabet and while I was getting used to the environment. But later on, things did improve.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: During the first few months -- during those first few months in Belgrade, where did you live?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, when we arrived from Bosnia, so it was in early August 1991, I lived with some friends of my mother and father's, Zoran and Kata Matijic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Where were your parents at the time?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Up until the 13th of September, my mom was in Zadar, and my dad, at that time, still lived in the barracks. My brother was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when your mother arrived in Belgrade, were you together?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: No. For a certain period of time, I think it was about a month and a half, we were apart. We lived in the same city but in three different places. My mom lived with -- with some other friends of ours, at Dolcol; I was with Aunt Kata and Uncle Zoki; and my father was in the barracks in Dedinje. It was only in November that we managed to rent an apartment. It was not until April 1992 that we got some premises from the army, and they then had to be refurbished in order to be fit for habitation, to turn them into a proper apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: During the period, so after you arrived in Belgrade and until the end of 1995, did you have any contact at all with your friends in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Throughout the war, I was in contact only with one friend, girlfriend. Up until the beginning of the war, we had been best friends and our friendship survived. She's a Croat; she remained in Zadar. In late 1991, she moved to Zagreb, and it was possible to exchange letters, to have a correspondence with Zagreb, because letters went through Hungary, so that we were able to exchange letters up until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you have any idea at all are where your father was between 1992 and the end of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Yes. My father was in the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Was he coming home every now and then?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Yes. He would come home approximately every three months. I can't now tell you that. But on the average, he would be home every three months, and then he would stay a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did he come in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, in 1995, just as he did in the previous years.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember until when he would have come to Belgrade in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: I think that he came, I think, in late March; and the next time the it was for my birthday, the 10th. He arrived a few days before my birthday, and he was in Belgrade then.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember the date of his arrival in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: He arrived on Friday. I remember that quite well because the 10th, my birthday, was on Monday that year. He arrived in -- on Friday, and that was the 7th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And what happened while he was there in Belgrade in July 1995? Can you describe the days that follow the 7th of July?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, well, just before that, I think in June - I can't give you the exact date - my father was promoted to the rank of general. So on the 7th, when he came home, he told us in the afternoon that he would like to celebrate the fact that he was promoted, and also my birthday, and perhaps the best thing would be to have a single feast to celebrate both occasions. So that afternoon, my father invited some of our family friends; and then on Saturday, the next day, and the day after that, we had people for lunch. And since the apartment was on the small side, the agreement was that my people, my friends, would come on the 10th, the day of my birthday, and they did come for the party on the 10th in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You told us that friends of the family arrived on the Saturday and the day after that.

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Why didn't the friends of the family come all in one go?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, the apartment was really small and it was simpler to divide them up over the period of two days.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You told us that your friends arrived on the 10th. Do you remember how you spent the day of the 10th and then the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I remember the 10th very well. As enrollment at the university was almost over, it was the last day that was possible, so I spent the whole morning at the university. In the evening, my friends arrived, and that was the first time I tasted alcohol, so all that really sticks in my memory. On the 11th, I slept in, which I didn't usually do in the morning. I remember that on the 11th, at around 6.00 or 7.00, my aunt rang up from Pale, and she spoke to my father. I know that. I remember that after that, Daddy was quite surprised and a little bit upset because she had told him that Srebrenica had fallen and he didn't know that before. Later on, at 7.30, it was announced on the news.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember when General Miletic left Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well, Your Honours. It was early in the morning of the 12th. I remember we said goodbye, I even remember what he was wearing, and I remember that I waved goodbye to him from the window. The whole scene is very vivid in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you go to Zadar after the war?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honours, I did, in the year 2000 and in the year 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you perhaps tells more about your relationship with your father, General Miletic. As a father, what he was he like?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was very lucky, I have to tell you, because my father was very understanding. We could communicate with few words. He's a very mild man. He is not a difficult man. We love each other very much, and we understand each other really well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci, Madam. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any of the Defence teams wishes to put questions? I would imagine there isn't anyone, so that's the position. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, just a very few questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Spiroski. My name is it Peter McCloskey, I represent the Prosecution, and I will just have a very few questions for you this morning. You said that your father's departure back to the war was a very vivid memory. Can you tell us who he went back to the war with, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Are you asking about July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That point after your birthday.

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I remember -- I don't know a lot about makes of cars, but I remember very well that it was a luxury car, black metallic in colour. This was unusual because Daddy didn't usually use a car like that, either when coming or going, but I don't remember whether there was anyone else inside the car. I waved to him from the window and watched him as he got into the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was he driving, or did he have a driver?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: No. He wasn't driving, Your Honour. There was a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was the driver?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I don't know. The driver did not get out of the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Had that car -- had your father arrived in that fancy car a few days earlier?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, when Daddy arrived in Belgrade, he arrived between 2.00 and 3.00 p.m. It was around lunchtime, and a driver came with him and we offered him lunch. That was usual. If somebody came with him, we would invite them to lunch, but I didn't go outside so I didn't see what sort of car he had used on arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was the driver that he arrived with the same driver that he left with a few days later?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, when Daddy was going back, the driver did not get out of the car, so I didn't see who the driver was. I saw the driver who came with him on arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, aside from those two brief times, did you see the driver? Did he come by to check in with your father or take him around town somewhere or anything like that that you remember?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's possible that he took him around town because on Monday, Daddy went out to do some errands. But I don't know whether that was the driver he went back with, because on the day he went back, the driver didn't come inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you make an effort to go look for any photos of your 18th birthday party and your father's celebration for becoming general?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, that was a very difficult time. Most of our belongings had been left behind in Zadar, so unfortunately I didn't have a camera. I would have loved to have taken photographs of many special times during my schooling; but, unfortunately, I was I wasn't able to and I wasn't able to do that on the birthday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, there were lots of adults and military folks, and we know from this case that they liked to do video, and people -- everybody likes to do video of special occasions and photographs. Did you make any effort yourself; or are you aware, did the Defence, in talking to you, did anyone make any effort to see if there is anymore record of this party or this weekend?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe the Defence lawyers tried to find that; but as for videos or photographs in our house, I would have known about that. But it's something I would love to have if such things existed. I wouldn't rest until I had got hold of those photos or videos, because that was a special family occasion for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we would like to have them, too. That's one thing we have in common, but sometimes those things don't exist. Were there any military people at that party your father had, any other colonels or generals?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There was Pero Djurdjic. I think he was a colonel at the time or a lieutenant-colonel, I am not sure. He was our Kum; then there was General Romanko Disevic with his wife; There was General - he is a general now; I don't know if he was then - Ivan Djoltic with his wife; and General Banjac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you have a television at your house then?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We got the TV set out of Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it worked okay during this period in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Yes, of course, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you had a telephone that worked, too?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was the television on, on the 10th, 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, from 1991 onwards, when we left Zadar, there was a TV show that we always watched in our house. That was the news at 7.30. We watched other news programmes also, but we never missed the news at 7.30, because my mother's and my father's families were both at risk, and we followed what the media recorded was happening in Croatia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember the station, what station that was, or the name of the programme that you would always watch?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Of course, it was the first programme, RTS, RST 1. They always had the main news programme at 7.30 and still do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, Doctor. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. McCloskey. Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, just one question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned a number of people who were there at the party back in July 1995. Were -- the people you mentioned, or some of the people you mentioned, were they all there on the same day, or were some there on one day and others on the other day?

utterances.speaker: MAJA SPIROSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't remember now who came on what day. The Prosecutor asked me about officers. There were also other people who were not officers, but we divided them up over two days.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no other questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are no further questions for you, Madam, which means your testimony finishes here. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over to give evidence, and on behalf of everyone here, I also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any documents? So no documents to tender. We can move to the next witness: Mr. Klacar.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have a little problem. We didn't think things would go so fast, so the following witness should be here at half past 12.00, but I'll try and make sure he can come early. Could we perhaps have a break now and possibly call the witness then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem. And in any case, we have no other option. So we'll have -- let's play it by ear. Would it be possible for you to check in good time when he could -- the earliest he could come, and then inform us accordingly. The sitting will resume as soon as he's back, all right? So, however, there will be at least a 20-minute break, at least, okay? Because that is regular. Registrar will communicate with everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am informed we have one housekeeping matter that might use the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That we can do, that we can do. Yes, Mr. Thayer. Take your time, we are not in a hurry.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you, and Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. Two housekeeping matters just to follow-up on; some issues that arose, I think, last week and even the week before. The first is, Your Honours, may recall during the cross-examination of General Simic, there was some confusion as to the date of the death of General Mladic's daughter. And I think we've arrived at an agreement with Defence Counsel. After searching various public media sources and other sources, that Ana Mladic, in fact, took her own life on the 24th of March, 1994. So I think we are able to stipulate among the parties that that was the date of that tragic incident. The second matter I wish to raise, I promised Judge Kwon I would be returning to the Court on this issue from last week, pertains to a question that our friends from the Gvero team raised in connection with the tendering of exhibits for witness Dragisa Masal. There was an order, a Main Staff order, which was shown to General Masal during his cross-examination. It was the same order that was entered into evidence through Richard Butler during his testimony. The version that was shown to General Masal was just a little different. It's one of the mischiefs that's created when we have the same document coming from different archives and sources and it gets a different ERN. So the question was raised, why was essentially the same document shown to two different witnesses with two different ERNs with slightly different markings on them. There is no great mystery. I simply pulled the document by ERN from one file that I have, didn't realise that Butler had been shown another version. Subsequently, there is no difference. There is some difference in markings, but the marks that were shown -- or that were on the document that were shown to General Masal are immaterial as far as the Prosecution is concerned. Given that, because that was the version that was shown to the witness, we would still ask that that second version be admitted, just so that we know exactly what indeed was shown to the witness, even though it's essentially the same document entered into evidence with Mr. Butler. The other issue related to that exhibit is, we had an English translation for the version shown to Mr. Butler, but no English translation of the version that was shown to General Masal. So we can get an English translation that also translates the very small handwriting on the version that was sent to or shown to General Masal, although it's, as far as the Prosecution is concerned, not an issue that we had any interest in raising. It simply says "to file" I think is the only difference in the handwriting shown to General Masal. So I just want to do update the Chamber to that, and the 65 ter document for the document in question is 2669 B, a Main Staff order dated 27 May 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Any comments, any objections to -- as regards the stipulation, I don't think there is anything you would like to say, as regards the other document that the Prosecution now wishes to tender for comparative purposes and for completion purposes. Okay, no comments. So go ahead, Mr. Thayer, and do what you said you will be doing. All right. We will break now. In the meantime -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am informed the witness will be here in ten minutes, but I need to -- I think we can still have the break now. It will be of 20 minutes -- 25 minutes. We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Klacar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've been summoned by General Miletic's Defence team to give evidence in this trial. Before you do so, however, you are required to make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. Madam Usher is going to give you the text. Please stand up, read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I begin? I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Is there nothing else? All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not for the time being. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Klacar. First I will introduce myself. As you know, my name is Nenad Petrusic; and today, I will be putting questions to you on behalf of the Defence of General Miletic. To begin with, please state your first and last name for the record?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
utterances.text: Ranko Klacar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I must also ask you at the outset to make a short pause between my question and your answer. It my be a good idea if you were to observe the cursor on the monitor, and when the cursor stops and the text is complete, you can begin your answer. Tell us, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: How old are you -- or, rather, what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
utterances.text: The 10th of April, 1962.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Klacar, observe the pause. Tell us, what school have you completed?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
utterances.text: I am a mechanical technician and a driving instructor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you work before the war?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
utterances.text: The military industry, Pretis Vogosca, near Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And where were you when the war broke out in 1992 on the territory of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
utterances.text: In Sarajevo at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
utterances.text: No, I fled. At the beginning of April, I moved to Serb-controlled territory -- or, what was it called at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What Serb-controlled territory did you move to? What town?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
utterances.text: I was referring to Sarajevo, but the area of Grbavica, and later on, Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were you conscripted into the army of Republika Srpska; and if so, tell us when?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
utterances.text: Yes, I was, on the 6th of May. That's when I joined the army of Republika Srpska, and I stayed there until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What unit did you join?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
utterances.text: The 2nd Romanija Battalion where I stayed for a few months, and then the rest of the war I spent at military post 3750 in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What duties did you have in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
utterances.text: I was a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: As a driver, what unit or sector did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
utterances.text: The rear, logistics; the part of the Main Staff that had to do with logistics and the rear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were you issued with a motor vehicle when you were working in logistics?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
utterances.text: Yes. In different periods of time, I was issued with different vehicles. So there was more than one vehicle, because this went on from 1992 to 1995. So I was issued with different vehicles, not all at the same time, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In 1995, when performing your job as driver in the Main Staff, were you assigned to different officers or only one officer?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
utterances.text: From 1993 onwards, I was mostly assigned to generals. And in 1994 and 1995, I was General Stevan Tomic's driver. He was a major-general, and he was the one whom I served the longest.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And what sector did Stevan Tomic belong to?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
utterances.text: He was - I don't know if I'll express myself properly - but he was the chief of finance or assistant commander for financial affairs. I don't know what is the proper military term for that. I'm only a driver, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you say the commander's assistant, are you referring to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what he was in terms of establishment, but he was the top man as far as finances went.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And where was his headquarters?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
utterances.text: His headquarters was in Crna Rijeka, and I was the only driver who was billeted elsewhere in relation to his immediate superior officer. I was in hotel Gora in Han Pijesak, and my immediate superior - the only one I reported to - General Tomic, was billeted in Crna Rijeka, seven or eight kilometres away in Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And then did you go from Han Pijesak to Crna Rijeka when summoned by General Tomic?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you recall in 1995 what vehicle were you using?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was a Golf MK II, it was quite new, it had come from the strategic stockpiles. It was virtually a new car. At the time when I got it, it had 40 kilometres. It was dark blue; we call it mouse colour. It's just one shade later than black; it's dark grey.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in the performance of your duties, did you rely on the transport and traffic service in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
utterances.text: Not directly. The drivers who drove generals were assigned to the generals. Both the vehicle and the driver were at the disposal of the general in question, and this general was not duty-bound to contact the transport and traffic service to ask for a vehicle. They, the generals, could use their vehicles and their drivers as needed. They didn't have to consult or ask for anything from the transport and traffic service. They didn't have to seek the service's approval. They only had to speak to their superiors if they wanted to go on a leave of absence or something like that, and they didn't have to look for any approval for the drivers and vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: As you drove General Tomic around the territory of Republika Srpska, did you receive travel orders or any similar papers?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In 1995, did you travel outside of the territory of Republika Srpska; or, to be more specific, did you travel to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how often?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
utterances.text: Well, I can say with absolute certainty that I went there more frequently than any other driver in the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you mean when you say that, "more frequently than any other driver"?

utterances.speaker: RANKO KLACAR
